A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
hyperpycnally fed turbidity currents can be used to record the rising and/or falling discharge of a river flood, but only for certain sediment grain sizes.

hyperpycnally driven turbidite systems may be more complex than previously thought and that future research should focus on the effects of river-flood dynamics on the formation of turbidity currents and the resulting deposits.
hyperpycnally deposited sand and mud are not necessarily good proxies for the timing and magnitude of a river flood, but they are good proxies for the temporal evolution of the river flood.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the link between fluvial discharge and hyperpycnal deposits can be complex and requires a detailed understanding of river-flood dynamics.
the sedimentary record of hyperpycnal turbidity currents can be complex and is not necessarily a direct record of the hydrograph of the flooding river.

hyperpycnally deposited sediment can be an effective record of river-flood dynamics, but this requires careful consideration of sediment size, river discharge, and the distance between the river mouth and the seabed.
